strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation from multi-view RGB/surface observations, an inverse problem not previously tackled at this level of anatomical detail.

SKIM dataset is a valuable, carefully engineered contribution: custom ArUco marker suit, high-resolution multi-layer anatomy (skin/muscle/bone), marker tracking pipeline with occlusion handling, and canonical correspondence construction — a useful resource for future biomechanics/vision research.

Technically sound method design: decoupled muscle/skin blendshape layers with a comprehensive set of biomechanically-motivated regularizers (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) that directly address the inherent ill-posedness/ambiguity of disentangling muscle vs. skin deformation from sparse markers.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation given the fundamental lack of dynamic in-vivo volumetric ground truth: multiple complementary metrics (global tracking, dynamic region error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) and comparisons against a kinematic lower bound (LBS) and a representative learned volumetric baseline (HIT).

Extensive and informative ablations (architecture choice, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that clarify the contribution of each design choice and show that naive fitting without priors leads to degenerate/implausible solutions.

Practical downstream utility demonstrated via a real-time visualization tool enabling per-muscle inspection, and a clear pipeline for propagating deformations to individual high-resolution muscle meshes usable in standard graphics engines.
Honest discussion of limitations (dependence on volumetric fitting initialization, marker-suit requirement, subject-specificity) rather than overselling the approach.
weaknesses: The dataset comprises only 5 subjects, and the model is explicitly subject-specific; this substantially limits claims of generalizability and the broader applicability of SOMA as a 'parametric' model in the conventional sense (i.e., generalizing across identities).

There is no direct ground-truth for internal muscle volume/shape during motion (e.g., dynamic MRI); all anatomical plausibility claims rely on proxy metrics (sparse marker residuals, volume preservation, intersection ratios) rather than validated internal muscle geometry, which is an inherent but still significant evidence gap for the core claim of 'recovering muscle deformations'.

The comparison to HIT may be somewhat mismatched, since HIT is a static, generic-template implicit model not designed for dynamic subject-specific tracking from sparse markers; the paper could benefit from additional baselines closer in spirit to the proposed task (e.g., simplified FEM or projective-dynamics baselines) to better contextualize the improvement.

Despite framing the method as 'scalable and cost-effective,' the data acquisition pipeline requires an expensive multi-camera markerless mocap studio (120 cameras), a separate 140-camera 3D body scanner, and a custom marker suit — this is a significant barrier to reproducibility and broader adoption that somewhat undercuts the stated practical impact, though this is acknowledged as future work (markerless capture).

Residual muscle-to-bone volume error remains relatively high (10.35%) even in the full model, and the paper's explanation (a 'realistic physical compromise') is plausible but not independently verified against any ground truth, leaving open whether this reflects genuine anatomical behavior or a modeling limitation.

The initial anatomical template relies on an existing volumetric fitting method [30], so errors or biases in that method propagate directly into SOMA's supervision signal and are not quantified independently in this work.
